accepted.reason: Good observation–target alignment: hospitalization rate plausibly tracks infections with a short lag, and delayed_I is explicitly recommended. With only 31 training weeks, avoiding an explicit H compartment reduces identifiability risk. A fixed 2-week delay is still simple (one extra knob) and is plausible for admissions timing; complexity remains low.

Also well-aligned with the hospitalization target via delayed_I and remains parsimonious/identifiable for short single-season data. Including a 1-week delay as a comparator is reasonable given uncertainty in the effective lag; risk is mainly peak timing sensitivity rather than structural mismatch.

rejected.reason: Fractional memory is not clearly justified by the series summary (single season, moderate peakiness, no zeros) and adds overfitting/identifiability risk in a short (31-week) training window. The expected failure mode (spurious persistence/instability) is particularly concerning for hospitalization-rate timing, where lag structure already provides temporal smoothing.

suggested_edits.edit: Clarify that the delay is intended to represent admission/reporting lag (not incubation), and note that a fixed delay may be a simplification if lag varies within-season.

State explicitly that the 1-week delay is included to bracket plausible admission lags (1–2 weeks) and to check sensitivity of peak timing; keep all other knobs identical to proposal 0 for clean comparability.

If retained at all, constrain the fractional component to be minimal (e.g., emphasize it as a sensitivity check only) and document a strong prior expectation of no improvement to reduce interpretability/overfitting risk; otherwise drop fractional for this short single-season series.
